To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
attentional biases to sad faces are associated with depression and to angry faces are associated with anxiety among youths.

youths with internalizing disorders (i.e., pure depression, pure anxiety, or comorbid depression and anxiety) exhibited attentional biases for sad or angry faces, whereas comorbed youths also exhibited attentional biases toward happy faces.
attentional bias to negative facial expressions was specific to pure depression and anxiety, whereas attentional avoidance of happy faces was specific to comorbid depression and anxiety.

the role of emotion processing in depression, and the specificity of this processing.
the role that attentional biases play in the development, maintenance and treatment of anxiety disorders and depression.
the development of the cognitive model in relation to depression and anxiety in children and adolescents.

the cognitive biases and processing that we observed are specific to pure internalizing disorders, and that these processes may be important for understanding etiological models of internalizing disorders in children and adolescents.

attentional biases for sad and angry faces are specific to depression and anxiety, respectively, in youths.
attentional biases to sad facial expressions may be a marker for clinical depression in youths, but not for generalized anxiety disorder.
